REPORT 
PART- I 
 
I. INTRODUCTORY 
The Public Accounts Committee decided to undertake a detailed examination 
of Para no. 3.4 of Comptroller and Auditor General Report No. 13 of 2018 relating to 
the Ministry of Defence (Department of Defence Production). The paragraph examines 
the subject “Delay in production of electronically upgraded 155mm/45 Calibre Gun 
System Dhanush”. 
2. In Para 3.4 of the C&AG Report, Audit has highlighted that the development of 
electronically upgraded 155mm/45 Calibre Gun System “DHANUSH” undertaken by 
Ordnance Factories (OFs) in the year 2011 was yet to be completely clear the user 
trials. As such, due to the delay in clearing user trials and consequent finalization of 
system configurations, the Bulk Production Clearance (BPC) for the indent of gun 
placed on OFB in March, 2013 was yet to be accorded by the Army. This further 
prolonged the wait of the Indian Army to hold modern artillery guns. 
3. The Committee took oral evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of 
Defence on the subject at their sitting held on 07th January, 2026 for in-depth 
examination of the issues related to the subject. on the basis of oral evidence and 
written information obtained from the Ministry on various aspects of the Audit Para 
under consideration, the Committee examined the subject as detailed in the 
succeeding paragraphs. 
 
II. AUDIT FINDINGS 
4. Artillery units of Indian Army hold 155mm/ 39 Calibre (towed) guns which were 
procured through a contract concluded in 1986 with M/s AB Bofors, Sweden the 
Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM). The contract also provide for Transfer of 
Technology (ToT) for upkeep & overhaul of the guns. 
5. According to Audit, since obtaining ToT in 1986-89, the OFB was producing 
certain assemblies/sub-assemblies. However, due to non-induction of any new 
artillery gun, and when deficiency in stock of 39 Calibre gun became sizable in 2009 
and the OEM offered old & used guns, the OFB stated its capability of producing gun 
based on ToT of 1986. Accordingly, Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) for procurement 
of a certain number of 155mm 39/45 Calibre gun as ‘Buy (Indian)’ from OFB with 
electronic &mechanical upgrade (to 45 Calibre) was accorded by Defence Acquisition 
Council (DAC) in October, 2011 and accordingly Project “DHANUSH” was started by 

2 
 
OFB. OFB was to produce two electronically upgraded prototypes of guns of 39 and 
45 calibre, respectively.  
6. However, during validation firing of the electronically upgraded gun which was 
carried out in May, 2012, the barrel and muzzle brake of gun was damaged. Based on 
the system validation check of 45 Calibre barrel and electronic sub system, fresh AON 
for another specified number of 45 Calibre guns, subject to successful completion of 
user trials was accorded by DAC in September, 2012 and the indent was placed on 
OFB in March 2013. 
7. Audit observed that evaluation of Automatic Gun Sighting System (AGSS) and 
Digital Intercom System of the gun by quality assurance agency was still in progress 
as of July, 2017. Audit also observed that during firing for user’s exploitation in July, 
2017, muzzle brake and related sub-systems failed and the investigations to identify 
the cause of accident was still being carried out during the month of July, 2017. 
8. Thus, the development undertaken by OFB in 2011 was yet to clear the user 
trials and as such the Audit further observed that the deficiency in holding of modern 
artillery gun continues and the Army is compelled to hold old guns with limited 
operation fire power.  
9. In light of findings of the audit, the Ministry of Defence (Department of Defence 
Production) submitted the following in their background note to theCommittee: 
9.1 “Development of ‘DHANUSH’ Artillery Gun System is a mega project of 
national importance involving various stakeholders i.e. govt. agencies and 
many Indian companies. The project is being continuously monitored in MoD. 
This is a weapon system of intricate and critical technologies. 
 
9.2 Dhanush Guns prototypes were ab-initio developed by OFB within 30 
months from the date of accord of the DAC decision on 07.10.2011 and were 
offered to the User for trials. OFB and the stakeholders have jointly worked to 
develop a world class and contemporary weapon system to fulfil the 
requirement of the User. It is worthwhile to mention that Dhanush was the first 
such gun developed in India, paving way for others to emulate. 
 
9.3 Normally similar gun systems are accepted as per the extant procedure 
by firing only 200 rounds and with one gun only as per the General Staff 
Qualitative Requirement (GSQR). Whereas, the weapon system “DHANUSH” 
has undergone most severe evaluations and trials ever conducted in the 
country to attain the best possible system in comparison to the available Gun 
System worldwide.  
 
9.4 Regarding the muzzle brake failure issue during firing for user 
exploitation in July 2017, a comprehensive defect investigation was carried out 

3 
 
which included qualification of sub-system as per international standards and 
STANAGs [Standardization Agreements of NATO]. Examination of affected 
equipment, ammunition and firing drill could not find any deficiency, which could 
cause / lead to incidents involving hitting of Muzzle brake by the exiting 
projectile. No single conclusive factor could be identified for incident / failure. 
This was possibly due to combination of several random factors causing chain 
of events leading to incident. During investigational firing at Proof and 
Experimental Establishment (PXE), Balasore, evidence of chances of 
occurrence of pressure oscillations, possibly, due to inconsistent burning of 
propellant was observed. Such pressure oscillations in a random event of 
differential pressure cyclic loading may lead to cyclic stressing of projectile body 
and may cause rupture / partial breakage of shell body and abnormal exit from 
barrel. Extensive firing was also carried out at PXE, Balasore. It was 
conclusively established in the enquiry report submitted in July 2018 by the 
Board of Officers, with representation from various stakeholders, that the failure 
of Muzzle Brake was not attributed to weapon system.  
 
9.5 The third and final phase of User Exploitation (UE) was successfully 
completed from 31st May 2018 to 7th June 2018 at Pokhran Field Firing Range 
(PFFR).  
 
9.6 After receipt of BPC in Feb 2019, ‘P’ no. of guns were issued in 
Mar’2019. Factory geared up for bulk manufacture of Dhanush Guns and 
manufactured all In-house sub-assemblies and positioned Inter Factory 
Demand (IFD) and Trade inputs for further ‘Q’ Guns. However, final integration 
was delayed due to non-availability of Electronic suite and Electrical System 
ex-BEL, which were made available in the month of Jan 2020. Out of total ‘Q’ 
Guns, ‘R’ Guns were sent for final proof at PXE Balasore by 20th Mar 2020, 
before nationwide lockdown due to COVID-19 pandemic was announced.  
 
9.7 Additional Secretary (DP) held a Review meeting with all the 
stakeholders on 29.07.2021. The various technical issues raised during the 
meeting were later resolved by the concerted efforts of all the stakeholders. 
 
9.8 BPC was granted and individual Guns were Passed in Proof. Further, 
the Induction of the gun was given a go-ahead after successful “Confidence 
Firing” on 8th March 2022 at PFFR Pokharan.  
 
9.9 In a major breakthrough for Indigenisation, the power pack which was 
earlier imported from foreign OEM, has now been replaced with an Indigenous 
power pack. The Guns with new power pack have already been issued to the 
User Units. This has alleviated import dependence and enable higher 
Indigenisation content. 
 

4 
 
9.10 Indent of ‘X’ no. of Guns was converted into Deemed Contract (Post 
Corporatization of OFB) having fixed Delivery schedule. Factory has 
manufactured and issued up to cumulative ‘A’ no of Guns and the remaining 
guns are expected to be delivered to Indian Army by year 2026.” 
 
 
III. Production Plan for Dhanush and Reasons for Delay. 
 
 
10.1  When asked about the original production plan and approved timeline for the 
electronically upgraded 155mm/45 Calibre Gun System Dhanush, the Ministry in their 
written reply submitted that the original production plan and timeline for delivery of the 
electronically upgraded 155mm/45 Calibre Gun System DHANUSH as per the original 
indent dated 4th March 2013placed by MoD(Acquisition wing), was 36 months after 
Bulk Production Clearance (BPC). Further, Post corporatization, the Deemed Contract 
was signed on 28/09/21 further amended on 10/10/2023, with following delivery 
schedule. AWEIL planned to issue all guns (cum-xx Nos) by March 2027.  
 
10.2  When asked to elaborate on the reasons for the delay in production of the Gun 
System, the Ministry in their written reply stated as under: 
 
“It is pertinent to mention that, the first two prototypes were made within 12 
months’ post Defence Acquisitions Council (DAC) clearance and detailed 
evaluation started thereafter. Based on the evaluation results, further 
prototypes were made and offered for evaluation. The evaluation methodology 
also evolved along with the production, as a Gun of this complexity was never 
made Indigenously nor evaluated. The trials underwent by Dhanush as part of 
development and trial phase are enumerated below: 
 

5 
 
 
 
It is pertinent to mention that Dhanush is the only gun to have been evaluated 
in 3 Gun formation [Troop Formation] and 6 Gun formation [Battery Formation] 
as per user’s request to fully conform the performance of the gun system. 
Generally, During the induction process for a gun fielded against RFP, the guns 
are evaluated as a single individual gun trial only, firing around 250 rounds. The 
BPC was accorded thereafter in Feb. 2019, and it was thus preceded by a 
complex development and trials and evaluation phase. It is also pertinent to 
mention that, the Development of Dhanush was the first ever such 
development, and many of the trials were also conceptualized and done for the 
first ever time.” 
 
10.3 When the Committee sought to know as to whether the Ministry made any 
reassessment of the roadmap for acquisition artillery because of the delay in 
production process of Dhanush, the Ministry in their written reply submitted as under: 
“Yes, the Indian Artillery has re-assessed the artillery acquisition roadmap from 
time to time based on operational requirement and pace of development of 
indigenous gun systems. The Indian Artillery, as per the revised roadmap has 


6 
 
included ATAGS (Advanced Towed Artillery Gun System), TGS (Towed Gun 
System), MGS (Mounted Gun System) & K9 Vajra-T (additional quantities) in 
its Artillery Profile to ensure that efforts of modernisation and indigenisation 
remain multi - pronged.” 
 
10.4 When the Committee enquired further to know the impact on the operational 
preparedness of the Army due to the delay and the arrangements made to bridge the 
capability gap, the Ministry in their written reply stated as under: 
 
“This gun development has come as a boost to Indigenous artillery 
development, and the project has been fully supported and guided by Artillery 
Dte. Though there had been a delay on account of reasons elaborated above, 
Arty has got a modern gun which can be supported Indigenously, and this is a 
long term and permanent strategic advantage. In fact, development of Dhanush 
has boosted the sustenance of Original Bofors Guns held in the Inventory of 
Arty, due to commonality and Indigenization of almost all the parts of original 
Bofors guns. 
 
Delay in production affected the operational preparedness of Army, particularly, 
Indian Artillery, however certain significant measures listed below ensured that 
voids are addressed and Army remains operationally ready – 
 
a. Upgunning of 130mm guns to 155mm/ 45 Cal Sharang & Soltam guns 
was undertaken. 
b. Induction of 155mm/ 39 Cal M777A2 UI-H guns ex USA. 
c. Indigenous development of 155mm/ 52 Cal ATAGS. 
d. Induction of K9 Vajra-T guns. 
e. Improvement in legacy guns for life extension.” 
 
10.5 To a query by the Committee regarding any cost escalation due to the delay in 
production, the Ministry in their written reply stated as under: 
“The issue price of Dhanush gun has been fixed as per mutually agreed 
Deemed Contract between AWEIL and Indian Army and there has been no cost 
escalation due to delay in production/issue of gun.” 

7 
 
 
10.6 On being further asked as to whether the delay led to idle capacity or unutilised 
funds, the Ministry in their written reply submitted as under:  
“There was no idle capacity nor any unutilized funds on account of this project.” 
 
IV. Role of OFB & Monitoring Mechanism for the Project 
 
11.1 With regard to the role of Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) in meeting production 
targets and their technical & infrastructural preparedness to undertake the project, the 
Ministry in their written reply stated as under: 
 
“The Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) served as the nerve center of this project, 
coordinating seamlessly with diverse stakeholders to ensure its continuous 
advancement. The intricate network of linkages established by OFB with other 
stakeholders is outlined below:
 
 
The Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) functioned as the headquarters for all units 
under its jurisdiction. In the development of the Dhanush Gun System, the Gun 
Carriage Factory (GCF) acted as the lead integrator, with support from 
approximately ten OFB units, as detailed below: 
 


8 
 
 
 
Hence, the role of OFB was to steer the project and monitor all those units, as 
above, to keep pace with the schedule and continue individual developmental 
push and production efforts. 
As this was the first such project of such a magnitude, being done through in-
house R&D, the infrastructure was not commensurate with the requirements to 
start-with. The infrastructure slowly augmented as experience was gained.” 
 
11.2 When the Committee sought to know about the monitoring mechanism put in 
place to oversee the  progress of the project, the Ministry in their written reply 
submitted as under: 
“The project was regularly monitored at the APEX level of erstwhile OFB and 
also seeing the importance of the same, Arty Dte/Indian Army organized an 
institutional mechanism by way of Technical oversight group (TOG) consisting 
of all the stakeholders. TOG has been guiding this project immaculately and 
has supported the gun through its long and elaborate journey.” 
 
V. Capacity Constraints or Skill Gaps. 
 
12.1 When asked as to whether any capacity constraints or skill gaps were identified 
during the project, the Ministry in their written reply stated as under: 
“Yes, it is to submit that no Arty Gun of this complexity and technological 
capabilities was ever made in India before this. Neither was there any supply 
chain existing which could have made components of this complexity. Dhanush 


9 
 
has contributed immensely to establishing a supplier and technical base to 
undertake development and production of Arty Guns. 
 
The major capacity constraints/skill gaps identified during the project were as 
under: 
a. Non-availability of Indigenous 155mm Barrel Design. 
b. Requirement of new Muzzle Brake for Dhanush gun. 
c. Non availability of Ballistics and other technical Expertise as it was the 
first gun to be manufactured indigenously. 
d. Non availability of Gun Electronics and expertise to integrate the same 
to the gun. 
e. Non availability of Navigation Systems and expertise to integrate the 
same to the gun. 
f. Non availability of technical expertise for integrating Advanced Sighting 
system with the Ballistic computer of the gun. 
g. Advanced automated systems such as auto-laying technology etc. for 
immediate deployment of the gun. 
h. Requirement of advanced Metallurgy such as indigenisation of micro-
alloy steel and converting standards to Indian equivalent standards. 
i. Indigenisation of other Critical Sub-systems like castings, forgings, and 
electronic relays 
All the above mentioned constraints/skill gaps were overcome by sincere efforts 
of erstwhile OFB and other stakeholders through indigenous sources and skills 
available with OFs and DPSUs. Dhanush has thus emerged as a symbol of 
self-reliance and capability building in India's defence paving the way for 
production of most advanced weapon system indigenously.” 
 
VI. Present Status of the Project and lessons learnt. 
 
13.1 When the Committee sought to know the present status of the Project, the 
Ministry in their written reply submitted as under: 
 

10 
 
“As on date [12/01/2026], total xx guns have been issued to Indian Army, with 
the project expecting to be get completed by March 2027 i.e. the total order of 
xx Nos. of Guns (given by Indian Army) will be supplied by March 2027.” 
 
13.2 On being asked about the lessons learned due to the delay in the project from 
2011 to 2026, the representative of the Ministry, during evidence before the Committee 
on 07thJanuary, 2026, responded as under: 
“...There are two parts to this. One is design and development, and the second 
is production. This product did not exist earlier. It was not designed in 2011. 
The first order was for design itself. At that time, in India, no such gun had been 
designed or manufactured. Even the sub-components had not been designed 
or manufactured. So, an assessment had to be made as to whether such a gun, 
with its sub-components, could be designed to be at par with global standards 
at that time. This was not twenty-year-old technology. Whether we could design 
it within a given time frame was an assumption. In hindsight, that assumption 
did not fully hold true. That criticism is fair.”  
 
13.3 On learnings from the project to ensure that such shortcomings are not repeated 
in future indigenous projects, the Ministry in their written reply further submitted as 
under: 
“The development of the Dhanush gun system has taught Indian Industry 
critical lessons in indigenous defence manufacturing: it gives a good learning 
experience and proved that a complex, modern artillery gun can be built 
domestically and hence created a roadmap for future self-reliance in 
development and manufacturing of advanced weapon systems using 
indigenous resources. 
Key Lessons/learnings from Dhanush Gun Development are elaborated as 
under: 
 
a. Indigenous Barrel Design: Successfully created a 155 mm, 23-litre 
chamber barrel entirely in-house, proving India's ability to independently 
design and manufacture complex artillery components. 
 
b. Muzzle Brake Innovation: Developed new analytical and design 
methods, enhancing recoil management and establishing a foundation 
for future indigenous shock-absorbing systems. 

11 
 
 
c. Ballistics Expertise: Achieved precise in-bore projectile analysis and 
ballistic calculations, strengthening domestic capability in advanced 
computational ballistics.  
 
d. Hydraulic Integration: Validated robust hydraulic systems capable of 
withstanding extreme shock, teaching resilience and reliability in artillery 
design. 
 
e. Gun Electronics: Integrated electronic controls with ballistic functions, 
marking a step toward digitized artillery and improved operational 
efficiency. 
 
f. Navigation Systems: Incorporated inertial navigation for enhanced 
mobility and deployment accuracy, reducing dependence on external 
aids. 
 
g. Advanced Sighting: Linked sighting systems with ballistic computers 
for real-time precision, demonstrating the value of integrated targeting 
solutions with day night capabilities. 
 
h. Automation: Introduced auto-laying technology, improving speed of 
deployment and reducing human error. 
 
i. Metallurgical Advances: Indigenised micro-alloy steel and adapted 
Swedish standards to Indian equivalents, strengthening local 
metallurgical expertise. 
 
j. Critical Sub-systems: Developed indigenous castings, forgings, and 
electronic relays, ensuring self-reliance in core components vital for 
strategic defence manufacturing. 
 

12 
 
The above learnings will prove beneficial in indigenous manufacturing of state 
of the art weapon systems and will greatly reduce the development time in other 
development projects in future.” 3

Part II 
OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Recommendation No. 1 
            The Committee note from the audit observations that the Artillery units 
of Indian Army hold 155mm/39 Calibre (towed) guns procured through a 
contract concluded in 1986 with AB Bofors, Sweden, the Original Equipment 
Manufacturer (OEM). The contract also provide for Transfer of Technology (ToT) 
which included indigenous production of the guns.  The Committee also note 
that due to a ban imposed by Ministry of Defence (MoD) in 1989 on the OEM for 
corruption charges, the Army pursued the case for procurement of guns of 
higher caliber (45/52) through open global tenders. The Committee observe, that 
however the Army did not manage to procure new artillery guns which were 
initiated in the 1990s due to issues viz. delay in deciding the actual requirement 
of guns, calibre, poor response of vendors, etc. and subsequently, the OFB was 
entrusted to produce two electronically upgraded prototypes of guns of 39 and 
45 calibre respectively, when deficiency in stock of 39 Calibre gun became 
sizeable in 2009. 
              The Committee find that the Ministry took two decades to finalise the 
procurement and induction of new artillery gun system resulting in huge 
deficiency in stock of the guns, which compelled the Army to hold old guns with 
limited fire power. It appears to the Committee that the Ministry do not have a 
proper mechanism or operating procedure to ensure periodical review and 
timely action for technological upgradation of existing gun systems or for 
procurement of new guns. The Committee are of the view that in the present 
geo-political scenario, the Ministry must be proactive to assess the stockpiles 
and efficacy of such critical guns to ensure that the armed forces are not 
deprived of credible equipments and technology. The Committee, therefore, 
recommend identification of capability gaps as per emerging threats at regular 
intervals and also take concrete steps to ensure timely acquisition of critical 
equipments and technology. 

14 
 
 
Recommendation No. 2 
         The Committee note from the submissions of the Ministry that the 
methodology for production of the Dhanush gun system evolved gradually 
alongwith the production process as such gun system had never been made 
indigenously. The Committee also observe that the existing infrastructure for 
production did not commensurate with the requirements for a project of such 
magnitude and all these factors led to the delay in the production process of 
Dhanush gun system. While the Committee appreciate the initiatives taken for 
indigenization of its defense sector which historically relied upon foreign 
suppliers, the Committee are not convinced by the submission of the Ministry 
attributing the delay in the production process to gradual development of 
evaluation methodology and lack of requisite infrastructure. The Committee 
urge upon the Ministry to critically and comprehensively assess the domestic 
capabilities vis-à-vis global market and the infrastructure requirements needed 
for undertaking production of indigenous defense systems beforehand, to 
reduce delays and prevent cost overruns. The Committee are of the considered 
view that steps for due assessment of technical and infrastructural 
preparedness for such indigenous ventures would go a long way in meeting the 
requirements of our forces and also help in reducing dependence on foreign 
suppliers. The Committee also recommend the Ministry to provide adequate 
support to domestic manufacturers for research and development (R&D) which 
will ultimately help us in making our defence system self reliant. 
 
Recommendation No.3 
 The Committee note that certain capacity constraints/skill gaps 
including,-(i) non availability of Ballistics & other technical expertise, (ii) non 
availability of gun electronics and (iii) non availability of technical expertise for 
integrating Advance Sighting system with the Ballistic computer of the gun, 
contributed to the delay in the production process. The Committee are also 
happy to note that all such constraints & skill gaps were overcame by sincere 

15 
 
efforts of erstwhile OFB and other stakeholders through indigenous sources 
and skills available with OFs and DPSUs.  
 While the Committee appreciate the efforts of the Ministry to fill the 
capacity & skill gaps through indigenous sources, the Committee are of the 
considered view that the challenges related to skill gaps & capacity constraints 
should have been flagged at the appropriate level during the approval stage, 
which could have led to better streamlining of the production process. The 
Committee therefore recommend that any constraints of capacity & skills 
related to indigenous production of defense weaponry must be taken into 
account and addressed before finalization of budgetary requirements & 
production schedule, as delays in production has the potential to render 
designs obsolete and adversely impacting the country’s quest for self reliance 
in the defense sector. The Committee also recommend for adequate attention to 
meet the gap in skills in the defence sector as apparent from the difficulties 
faced in the production process of Dhanush. The Committee recommend that 
the Ministry explore the possibility of introducing specially designed skill 
development courses in various technological institutes including IITs to 
develop a skilled workforce, as per requirements of the country’s indigenous 
military program. The Committee are of the view that such measures can also 
have broader positive ramifications in terms of economic impact on industrial 
growth and creation of jobs.   
 The Committee further recommend the Ministry to work out a mechanism 
for upskilling the existing manpower of Defence Public Sector Undertakings 
(DPSUs) at regular intervals to enable them to upgrade their skills and 
knowledge in line with the country’s efforts to match with major defense 
manufacturing countries of the world in terms of producing cutting edge 
weaponry for our defense forces to tackle emerging threats. 
 
Recommendation No. 4 
 The Committee have noted the submission of the Ministry that the 
Dhanush gun system has boosted the sustenance of Original Bofors Guns held 

16 
 
in the Inventory of the Army, due to commonality and Indigenization of almost 
all the parts of original Bofors guns. However, the Committee are also 
concerned to note the admission of the Ministry that the delay in production 
affected the operational preparedness of the Army, specially the Artillery 
Division. Considering current geopolitical scenario, the Committee are of the 
opinion that the Indian Army cannot function with obsolete artilleries for such a 
long period of time and therefore recommend that the Ministry take concrete 
steps towards structural transformation of the decision making process, so that 
such matters of national security are not marred by unrealistic delays. The 
Committee also urge upon the Ministry to focus on supply chain management 
and formulation of guidelines or SOPs to ensure that suppliers meet the criteria 
as per the operational requirements of the armed forces, and also to ensure that 
such suppliers adhere to timelines as may be specified in the respective 
contracts. 
Recommendation No. 5 
 The Committee note that the Dhanush project was regularly monitored at 
the APEX level of erstwhile OFB and that considering the importance of the 
project, the Artillery Division of the Indian Army created  an institutional 
mechanism called the Technical Oversight Group (TOG) consisting of all the 
stakeholders to guide the project. The Ministry has submitted before the 
Committee that Indian Army re-assesses the artillery acquisition roadmap from 
time to time based on operational requirements and pace of development of 
indigenous gun systems.  
 While the Committee acknowledge the efforts of the Ministry through 
various monitoring mechanisms to oversee the progress of the Dhanush 
project, they have also observe that inspite of the monitoring mechanisms as 
stated by the Ministry, the project has missed several deadlines for its 
completion. Considering the fact that the weapon system is first of its kind being 
produced in the country, the Committee, recommend that the Ministry explore 
the possibility of additional measures that may required to be taken for ensuring 
that the project do not face further hurdles and is completed in a time bound 
manner within the extended timeline i.e, March, 2027. The Committee also 

17 
 
further recommend that the Ministry take necessary steps to ensure that all the 
stakeholders involved in the project, specially the AWEIL which is responsible 
for manufacturing and system integration of the Dhanush system to be 
proactive, and to anticipate possible disruptions specially due to mechanical 
and technological issues, focus on efficient management of the supply chain 
and optimization of the workflows.

 I, the Chairperson, Public Accounts Committee (2026-27) having been authorized by

62.10 crore on replacement of defective ammunition to Army by Ordnance Factory, Badmal” 
based on Para 3.5 of Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG) Report No. 15 of 2019 
relating to the Ministry of Defence (Department of Defence Production). 
2.  The C&AG Report No. 15 of 2019 was laid on the Table of the House on 06.12.2019. 
3.  The Sub-Committee - II on “Defence” was constituted by the Public Accounts 
Committee (2025-26) for detailed examination of the subjects related to Ministry of Defence.

PAC and Member of Parliament, Lok Sabha. Public Accounts Committee (2025-2026) 
selected the aforesaid subject and allocated the same to Sub-Committee – II (Defence) for 
examination and Report.

briefing by Audit on 03.11.2025. Thereafter, Sub-Committee took oral evidence of the

aforementioned subject on 07.01. 2026. The Sub-Committee considered and adopted the

adopted by the Public Accounts Committee (2026-2027) during their sitting held on

5.  For facility of reference and convenience, the Observations and Recommendations of 
the Committee have been printed in bold and form Part-II of the Report.

26) for taking oral evidence and obtaining information on the subject

1 
 
REPORT 
PART- I 
I. INTRODUCTORY 
The Public Accounts Committee decided to undertake detailed examination of 
Para no. 3.5 of Comptroller and Auditor General Report No. 15 of 2019 relating to the 
Ministry of Defence (Department of Defence Production). The paragraph examines 
the subject “Loss of Rs. 62.10 crore on replacement of defective ammunition to Army 
by Ordnance Factory, Badmal”. 
2. In Para 3.5 of the C&AG Report, Audit has highlighted that the Ordnance 
Factory, Badmal (OFBL) supplied to Army two types of 155 mm ammunition in March, 
2009 & March, 2010, respectively. However, Army reported exudation of TNT mix 
explosives from the shells of ammunition within their shelf life. This was on account of 
lower set point (melting point) of TNT than the specified range, and that requisite test 
of set point value of TNT in TNT mix were not carried out at OFBL before filling in shell 
due to the absence of provision for such testing in the specification of Controllerate of 
Quality Assurance (CQA). Consequently, it led to a loss of Rs.62.10 crore on account 
of replacement of defective ammunition by the OFB.  
3. The Committee took oral evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of 
Defence on the subject at their sitting held on 07th January, 2026 for in-depth 
examination of the issues related to the subject. On the basis of oral evidence and 
written information obtained from the Ministry on various aspects of the Audit Para 
under consideration, the Committee examined the subject as detailed in the 
succeeding paragraphs. 
 
II. AUDIT FINDINGS 
4. Ordnance Factory, Badmal (OFBL) is a filling factory of 155 mm artillery 
ammunition. In manufacturing of the ammunition, Tri Nitro Toluene(TNT) is used as 
explosive. OFBL receives TNT (special grade) as input from High Explosives Factory 
(HEF), Kirkee. TNT (special grade) is mixed with other additives at OFBL before filling 
shells of the ammunition. 
5. According to the Audit, OFBL had issued (March 2009 and March 2010) 155 
mm ammunition to Army at a cost of Rs. 43.62 crore and Rs. 16.53 crore respectively. 
The ammunitions were issued after quality check by Quality Control Cell of OFBL and 
quality audit & surveillance check by Senior Quality Assurance Officer (Ammunition) 
Badmal under DGQA. 
6. However, in April, 2014, exudation from shells of the ammunition was reported 
by Field Ammunition Depot (FAD), Jodhpur. Consequently, chemical analysis of 
exudative shells by Controllerate of Quality Assurance (Military Explosives) (CQA), 

2 
 
Khadki (Pune) revealed (June, 2017) that exudation was due to low purity of TNT with 
set point (melting point) below 80.6 degree centigrade and higher vacuum stability 
than the prescribed range. CQA (A), Khadki, therefore, sentenced a total of 21,259 
quantity of both types of ammunition as unserviceable. 
7. Audit has also highlighted that the indent issued by Army in October, 2008 
contained a condition that in case the ammunition failed to perform as per the 
specification during the shelf life (15 years) or reported defective, the supplier (OFB) 
would either rectify or replace the same free of cost. Accordingly, 14,159 ammunition 
were replaced free of cost by OFBL. The Audit has estimated the total financial 
involvement for replacement of the ammunition at about Rs. 62.10 crore at the issue 
price of 2018-19. 
8. Audit has noted that specification for TNT mix did not stipulate any provision to 
measure set point TNT mix. However, CQA had stated that by not mentioning set point 
clause in the specification does not mean to refrain from set point testing. 
9.        Audit has also noted that TNT is a highly inflammable chemical and that its 
exudation had primarily caused major fire accidents at CAD, Pulgaon in 2016. Thus, 
the  Audit has recommended the Factory and the DGQA to resolve the testing methods 
for such highly inflammable materials. 
10. In light of findings of the audit, the Ministry of Defence (Department of Defence 
Production) submitted the following in their background note to theCommittee: 
10.1 “OFBL manufacture 155mm ammunition since 1998 having Tri Nitro 
Toluene (TNT) mix as explosive filling. TNT has been manufactured by High 
Explosive Factory (HEF) Pune since 1944-45. TNT, manufactured at HEF has 
been despatched to OFBL where the specific grade of TNT is mixed with other 
ingredients to manufacture High Explosive (HE) mix. During pre-corporatization 
of OFB, the quality assurance was being done by Controllerate of Quality 
Assurance (Ammunition) to ensure the quality of TNT manufactured at HEF 
strictly as per relevant specification.  
 
10.2 It is submitted that DGQA, the quality assurance establishment, 
confirmed that the Set point of TNT will not be altered by addition of additives. 
Hence, once the Set point is determined at HEF, its further determination at 
OFBL is technically unwarranted. Therefore, there was absence of any 
stipulation in the governing specification as well as test facility to check the Set 
point of TNT mix again at OFBL. 
 
10.3 Since there was no ambiguity regarding testing methods of TNT and no 
deviation from standard specification took place, the question of fixing of 
responsibility does not arise. However, after receipt of customer feedback in 
instant case, OFBL had introduced additional tests to measure Set point value 

3 
 
of TNT mix of all the Lots and grades, since December 2016, as a corrective 
action.  
 
10.4 Presently, rigorous testing of all the lots of TNT is being done at HEF 
Pune and lots cleared in testing being issued to OFBL for further processing 
and filling of ammunition. At OFBL, the Set point of TNT mix of all the lots are 
again checked before filling the mix in the ammunition. In addition, crimping 
operation was added for the Aluminium Liner during assembly of Shell. SQAE 
further ensures the quality of TNT mix and the ammunition during FAI of end 
product at OFBL as per relevant specification and no case of lowering of set 
point or exudation of TNT has been observed during FAI of the ammunition at 
OFBL. Further, after implementing the said preventive measures, no complaint 
of occurrence of TNT Exudation has been received from the lots manufactured 
by OFBL.” 
 
III. Quality Assurance and Inspection Mechanism for the Ammunition. 
 
11.1 In the light of Audit findings, the Committee asked about the mechanism for 
inspection and quality assurance at OF, Badmal. The Ministry in their written reply 
submitted as under: 
 
a. “A well-defined Quality assurance and inspection mechanisms were in 
place at Ordnance Factory, Badmal at the time of manufacturing.In this 
regard, the various control points and surveillance points were identified 
in the manufacturing process wherein the inspections were being carried 
out by factory Quality Control (QC) and Director General Quality 
Assurance (DGQA). 
b. The inspection and testing of raw materials were carried out by Quality 
Assurance Materials Group of the factory. 
c. During manufacturing of the ammunition,the inter stage inspection were 
carried out by factory QC and DGQA at various predefined critical control 
points and surveillance points. 
 
d. After completion of manufacturing, the Final Acceptance Inspection (FAI) 
was carried out by DGQA. The samples were drawn as per predefined 
sampling plan under IS 2500 and the samples were subjected to proof 
firing at proof ranges and other Qualifying Tests were carried out. 
e. Quality assurance activities were performed by DGQA representatives 
stationed at Ordnance Factory Badmal (OFBL).” 
 
 

4 
 
11.2 When the Committee sought to know the role played by DGQA in the instant 
case and as to whether any inspection protocols were diluted, bypassed or 
inadequately implemented, the Ministry in their written reply responded as under: 
 
“DGQA, the independent authorized department under MOD ensured Quality 
Assurance on behalf of Indian Army for all the products supplied to Indian 
Army.The role of DGQA was to provide Quality Audit and Surveillance(QA&S) 
on sampling basis as per Quality Assurance Plans (QAP), relevant technical 
specifications and proof schedule. None of the QA&S procedures/ Inspection 
protocol was diluted/ by passed or inadequately implemented.” 
 
 
11.3 Elaborating further on the inspection protocols followed, the representative of 
the Ministry during the evidence held on 7th January informed the Committee as under: 
“Coming to this point of exudation which has been observed in the ammunition, 
the cause of this exudation is basically and fundamentally the explosive, which 
is TNT. This TNT is produced in one factory and it is transported to another 
factory where it is filled. In ordnance factory, Badmal, it is filled inside the 
ammunition. This ammunition, when it went to the army depot, they found this 
exudation phenomenon after four years. As far as the quality control and quality 
assurance is concerned, we have a dual responsibility. There are certain areas 
which are looked into by the manufacturer himself. When he buys the materials, 
the purity of the material what he buys and all those aspects are ensured. They 
give the report to us. Then when they make a final product, DGQA tests it. It is 
an important and critical test and we find that these critical tests are okay or 
not. In the instant cases of problem which has been observed, we re-verified all 
the cases with all the data which was available. We found that there were no 
aberration and everything was alright.” 
 
11.4 When the Committee enquired as to how the defective ammunition managed 
to clear internal quality checks, the Ministry in their written reply stated as under: 
a. “TNT was manufactured at HEF Khadki and 100% checks were carried out 
by QC Ordnance Factory. The resident Directorate General of Quality 
Assurance (DGQA) establishment carried out quality Audit and 
Surveillance (QA&S) at selected and mutually agreed control point stages. 
The TNT set point (80.6°C) test was carried out by the resident DGQA 
establishment on the samples drawn from 1000kg of TNT(50 boxes@ 20 
kg for box) and found acceptable. 
b. The TNT was supplied by HEF, Khadki to OFBL. Later, OFBL had mixed 
the TNT with additives before filling in the Shell. Set point of TNT will not be 

5 
 
altered by addition of additives. Hence, once the Set point is determined at 
HEF, its further determination at OFBL is technically not required.  
c. The TNT mix was then filled into 155mm shell at OFBL. The Ammunition 
Lotswere cleared after 100% QC checks by OFBL QC department and 
QA&S checks at selected points as per Quality Assurance Plans (QAP) by 
resident DGQA Establishment on sampling basis. 
d. As explained above, the ammunition which has cleared multiple levels of 
Inspection at various stages of manufacture and finally after successfully 
passing of proof firing, I-Note (Inspection Note) has been issued by the 
independent Quality Assurance agency, DGQA, before acceptance and 
dispatch of the ammunition to the Indian Army.” 
 
 
11.5 With regard to a query on whether any systemic deficiencies in manufacturing, 
testing or oversight have been identified in OF, Badmal, the Ministry in their written 
reply submitted as under: 
 
“....the ammunition was manufactured strictly as per approved specifications, 
process schedules, and QAP. Quality control and quality assurance checks 
were carried out at every stage of manufacturing, testing, and inspection. No 
systemic deficiencies were Identified..... after receipt of customer feedback in 
instant case, OFBL had introduced additional tests to measure Set point value 
of TNT mix of all the Lots and grades, since December 2016, as a corrective 
action. In addition, crimping operation was also added for the Aluminium Liner 
during assembly of Shell at OFBL to eliminate any possibility of such incidence 
in future.” 
 
 
11.6 To a specific query of the Committee regarding fixing of responsibility in the 
case, the Ministry in their written reply responded as under: 
“The concerned ammunition was supplied to Indian Army after clearing of 
multiple levels of inspection at various stages of manufacture and after 
successful proof firing. The ammunition was supplied to Indian Army after all 
the quality tests/trials were passed and cleared by the independent Quality 
Assurance agency, DGQA. In view of the fact that the ammunition supplied to 
the Indian Army complied with all the prescribed quality standards, the issue of 
fixing responsibility did not arise in the case. Further, after receipt of customer 
feedback in instant case, OFBL had introduced additional tests to measure Set 
point value of TNT for all the Lots and grades, since December 2016, as a 
corrective action. In addition, crimping operation was also added for the 
Aluminium Liner during assembly of Shell at OFBL to eliminate any possibility 
of such incidence in future.” 

6 
 
 
IV. Guidelines or Policy on Defective Ammunition. 
 
12.1 When the Committee sought to know of the provisions in the contract to deal 
with such cases of supply of defective ammunition and as to whether the provision 
was invoked, the Ministry in their written reply submitted the following information: 
 
“As per the conditions in the Indent that in case of Ammunition fails to perform 
as per the specification during shelf life (15 years) or reported defective, the 
supplier (erstwhile OFB) would either rectify or replace the same. Accordingly, 
erstwhile OFB/MIL provided the replacement of the ammunition in the instant 
case.” 
 
12.2 With regard to steps taken to ensure supply of zero-defect ammunition in future, 
the Ministry in their written reply stated as under:  
 
“Munitions India Limited (MIL) is following international quality assurance 
standards. Acceptance Quality Limits (AQL) and sampling plans are 
implemented as per IS-2500 standards. All Quality Assurance Plans (QAPs) 
are vetted by DGQA. QAPs and Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) are in 
place, further, in certain cases where continued quality issues are observed, 
quality audit is being carried out and the revision, if required, is being made in 
consultation with DGQA to ensure continual improvement.” 
 
12.3 Further with regards to concerns of the Committee with regard to the necessity 
for supplying defect free ammunition to the Army, the representative of the Ministry 
during Evidence held on 7th January, 2026, explained as under: 
“The second aspect is when this good item went to the ordnance factory, 
Badmal it got filled up. During the filling process, they have to take care of 
certain things and then they should do the filling process. But notwithstanding 
that time also we did a lot of check like whether the filling is proper, if the crack 
is there, or if porosity is there, whether density is okay, all these parameters 
also had been checked and that also we found it okay. After four years, this 
phenomenon had exhibited. There is one chemical aspect of TNT and it has 
got a natural tendency, in case of any impurities which are present inside the 
explosive, these impurities will exhibit this phenomenon after a lapse of time. It 
cannot be detected at the instant case during the manufacture, but after a lapse 
of time.So, in the instant case the 19 FAD which was there in Rajasthan, where 
the temperature goes to 50-55 degree centigrade, after four years they found 
that there is something leaking. That is due to the impurities which has caused 

7 
 
this problem. But we tried to derive from the quality point of view, wherever the 
documents were available. But all the documents were in order both from the 
manufacturing side as well as the QA side. Then, what remedial measures and 
the preventive measures we needed to immediately implement had been 
addressed through a task force. The task force has given various directions for 
both the manufacturer of the explosives as well as the explosives.” 
 
12.4 Responding to the specific query of the Committee on the outcome of 
suggestions given by the task force, the Representative of the Ministry submitted as 
under: 
“The task force was constituted by the QA agency. They studied it, and then 
our chemical military explosive experts also analyzed everything. After the 
analysis, they given the various suggestions how it can be improved upon. So, 
based on the improvement only, they have implemented in the 
factories…….After this, we have not experienced this.” 
 
 
V. Ordnance Factory, Badmal and DGQA 
 
13.1 When the Committee asked for the details of performance of Ordnance Factory, 
Badmal (OFBL) during the last five years, the Ministry in their written reply submitted 
as under: 
 
“OFBL is a critical production unit supplying Large calibre ammunition to the 
Indian Army, including 155 mm. 130 mm. 125 mm. and 105 mm ammunition, 
which are vital for the Artillery Division. OFBL has supplied various types of 
ammunition valuing Rs. 3,098 Crore during the last 5 years (2020-21 to 2024-
25) to Indian Army. Also, ammunition valuing Rs. 475 Crore has been exported 
to friendly foreign countries(export authorised by GoI) during last 5 years (2020-
21 to 2024-25) without any Quality Issues being reported.” 
 
13.2 Responding to query of the Committee about the sanctioned and present 
strength of officials in the DGQA, the Ministry in their written reply furnished following 
information:

PART II 
OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Recommendation No. 1 
 The Committee note from the audit observations that the Ordnance 
Factory, Badmal (OFBL), which is a unit of Munitions India Limited (MIL) had 
supplied two types of 155 mm ammunition to the Army in March, 2009 and 
March, 2010, respectively and that the Army reported exudation of TNT mix 
explosives from the shells of ammunition within their shelf life, due to lower set 
point (melting point) of TNT than the specified range. The Committee also note 
that required test of set point value of TNT in TNT mix were not carried out at OF 
Badmal before filling in shell due to absence of provision for such testing in the 
CQA’s specification. OFB had to give free replacement of 14,159 ammunition to 
Army resulting in loss of Rs. 62.10 crore on account of replacement of defective 
ammunition by the OFB. 
 The Committee observe that there was no provision for testing of TNT mix 
in the Controllerate of Quality Assurance (CQA) specification for such a crucial 
ammunition being supplied to the Indian Army.  The Committee are of the view 
that non inclusion of testing provisions for the ammunition points towards 
lacunae on the part of the OFBL, CQA, DGQA and the Ministry as a whole with 
regard to the methodology and mechanism being adopted by them for 
inspection and evaluation of arms and ammunitions being produced to ensure 
quality assurance. The Committee note that after receipt of customer feedback, 
OFBL had introduced additional tests to measure set point value of TNT for all 
lots and grades since December 2016, as a corrective action. The Committee 
therefore recommend the Ministry to duly revisit the relevant provisions related 
to specifications for testing or method for testing of various ammunitions which 
are currently under development at various OFs to ensure that all such products 
are subjected to stringent quality tests and trials and thereby to prevent 
recurrence of such incidents. The Committee also recommend the Ministry to 
review the collaboration and coordination mechanism being followed between 

10 
 
various stakeholders and also to improve the functioning of OFB to build a more 
robust and credible checking as well as testing methodology to ensure that our 
defence forces are supplied with quality ammunitions. The Committee firmly 
believe that such measures for quality control are of utmost necessity to prevent 
ammunition related accidents in the field, which can cause injuries and fatalities 
to personnel handling them and also restore confidence amongst the armed 
forces with regard to ammunitions being manufactured by OFB.  
 
Recommendation No. 2 
 The Committee note from the submission of the Ministry that the 
Munitions India Limited (MIL) follows international quality assurance standards 
and as per IS-2500, and also that all Quality Assurance Plans (QAPs) are vetted 
by DGQA. The Committee also note that the concerned ammunition was 
supplied to the Indian Army after clearing multiple levels of inspection at various 
stages of manufacture and after successful proof firing. The Committee further 
note that all the quality tests and trials for the ammunition were passed and 
cleared by the independent quality assurance agency- DGQA (Directorate 
General of Quality Assurance) and that additional test to measure Set point 
value of TNT for all lots and grades were introduced later after receipt of 
customer feedback.  
             The Committee find it concerning that even after various levels of 
inspection during manufacturing of the ammunition at Ordnance Factory 
Badmal, and trials and tests having cleared by DGQA, the final product supplied 
to the Army turned out to be defective. The Committee are of the considered 
view that the incident highlights the presence of major gap between trials and 
testing protocols of ammunition and its actual performance in the field. 
  In a broader perspective, the Committee, therefore, recommend the 
Ministry to review the whole methodology of testing by the quality control 
department of the OFs, CQA and DGQA, including the method of sampling. The 
Committee urge the Ministry to explore the possibility of testing multiple 
samples for certification of an ammunition. The Committee also recommend that 

11 
 
the inputs/ materials being used for production of the ammunition must also be 
stringently checked to ensure that end products are of the utmost quality. The 
Committee further recommend the Ministry to duly examine the technical as well 
financial competency of the concerned manufacturers before awarding such 
high value projects.  
 
Recommendation No. 3 
 The Committee note that the DGQA ensures Quality Assurance on behalf 
of Indian Army for all products supplied to the Indian Army. The Committee also 
note that in the instant case the role of DGQA was to provide Quality Audit and 
Surveillance (QA&S) on sampling basis as per Quality Assurance Plans, 
technical specifications and proof schedule, and also that none of these 
procedures and protocols were diluted or bypassed.  However, the Committee 
are not convinced with the submission of the Ministry with regard to 
accountability in the case, wherein they have stated that the issue of fixing of 
responsibility in the case do not arise as the ammunition complied with all the 
prescribed quality standards.  The Committee are of the considered view that 
such matters are related to national security and lack of accountability for poor 
quality of arms ammunition are not in national interest, as it has potential to 
adversely impact the operational preparedness of the Army. 
 
 The Committee, therefore, recommend the Ministry to strengthen the 
mechanism of accountability in such cases where ammunitions turn out to be 
defective after clearing all necessary tests as per stipulated specifications or if 
detected by the end users at the field level. The Committee further recommend 
the Ministry to comprehensively examine all such cases of ammunition 
accidents in recent years, including the instant case, to identify the basic 
reasons and pattern of ammunition accidents, which will enable the concerned 
stakeholders to make necessary improvements in the products as well as on the 
kind of additional tests or trials that may be required for ensuring quality 
assurance. The Committee further urge upon the Ministry to take steps for 
studying and adoption of global best practices with regard to testing 

12 
 
methodologies. The Committee would like to be apprised of the action taken by 
the Government in this regard. 
 
Recommendation No. 4 
 The Committee have been informed of the presence of a well defined 
Quality assurance and inspection mechanism at the Ordnance Factory, Badmal 
(OFBL), by the Ministry. The Committee note the audit observations which 
states that the ammunition were issued following quality check by the Quality 
Control Cell of OFBL and by the Senior Quality Assurance Officer of DGQA. The 
Committee also note with satisfaction that the OFBL has supplied various types 
of ammunition worth Rs. 3,573 crore, including to certain friendly foreign 
countries, during the last five financial years.  
 However, the Committee are of the view that the Quality Control (QC) cell 
of Ordnance factories including OFBL, the erstwhile OFB and DGQA are 
perhaps not performing at the desired level of expectations, as exemplified by 
the instant case. There also appears to be a perceptible gap at both factory level 
and DGQA inspections of ammunition. The Committee, therefore, recommend 
that the Ministry take steps to review the overall functioning & performance of 
DGQA and Directorate of Ordnance (erstwhile OFB), which is the main source 
of supply of arms and ammunition to our strong Army, to further strengthen 
their roles and responsibilities. The Committee believe such review is of utmost 
necessity, as India is pitching for self reliance in the defence sector through 
various initiatives including the Make in India initiative. The Committee further 
recommend the Ministry to take steps to well equip the OFs, DGQA and other 
related organizations with ever evolving and emerging advanced technologies 
including AI to enable them to discharge their responsibilities efficiently.  
          The Committee also note that around 62% of the sanctioned strength of 
various posts of Group A, B and C under DGQA and its various establishments 
are lying vacant. The Committee find it quite surprising that the organization 
whose primary responsibility is to ensure quality control and quality assurance 
of arms and ammunitions being produced by various Ordnance Factories is 
functioning with less than half of its sanctioned strength.  

13 
 
            The role and responsibilities entrusted upon DGQA make it incumbent 
upon its officials to conduct inspections, testing and certifications, and also 
offer assistance to manufacturers in meeting standards of products, for which 
the Committee believe will require constant visit by the concerned officials to 
the project sites and testing facilities, which are located at different parts of the 
country. The Committee are of the considered view that without sufficient 
manpower, the DGQA may not be able to discharge its responsibilities 
efficiently and in a time bound manner, due to unbalanced workload on 
incumbent officials. The Committee, therefore, recommend the Ministry to take 
immediate steps to fill up all the vacant posts and also pursue strongly with the 
concerned recruitment agency to complete the process expeditiously. Given the 
critical nature of quality assurance in defence production, the Committee cannot 
rely on open-ended assurances regarding recruitment. The Committee direct the 
Ministry to submit a time-bound, phase-wise institutional roadmap, detailing 
specific targets for recruitment and the structural reorganization of the DGQA.

9.         The Committee had observed a persistent delay in the construction 
of Road Over Bridges (ROBs). Based on the responses from the Ministry 
of Railways, the Committee believe there are significant lapses in the 
regulatory and compliance mechanisms between the Ministry and the 
State Government of Maharashtra, particularly since directives were 
issued by the Ministry in 2008. The Committee note that the Railway 
Administration failed to secure the necessary commitments from the State 
Government regarding LC No. 144 at Mhasawad. This failure not only 
contravened official directives but also resulted in a blockage of capital 
expenditure amounting to Rs. 18.75 crores due to the incomplete work on 
the State's part. 
The Ministry’s justification that simultaneous work on both portions of the 
ROB indicates the State Government’s commitment is found by the 
Committee as questionable. The prolonged delays, primarily attributed to 
land acquisition and court cases, could have been mitigated if the Ministry 
had enforced a more stringent compliance mechanism and initiated 
effective consultations from the outset. Moreover, the Committee highlight 
the numerous communications between the Railways and the State Public 
Works Department (PWD), which reveal a bureaucratic stalemate. In 
response to the Committee’s recommendation that the Ministry identify 
the officials responsible for failing to engage in the necessary consultation 
process prior to project execution, the Ministry stated that no individual 
could be held accountable. The Committee find it surprising that, despite a 

6 
 
delay of over four years and the blocking of public funds amounting to Rs. 
18.75 crores, the Ministry's assertion that no one is individually 
responsible raises several concerns.  
  
While the Committee acknowledge the external challenges, such as land 
acquisition issues and court cases, the failure to hold anyone accountable 
reflects a broader failure of governance and oversight. Therefore, the 
Committee recommend identifying officials accountable for the Ministry's 
failure to secure commitments from the State Government and to actively 
engage with them. The ROB project, originally expected to be completed 
within 18 months, has now extended over eight years. The Ministry's 
stance that the Railway portion of the ROB was completed in 2016, while 
the State Government's delay in finishing the approach road halted the 
project, suggest that Railway authorities are more focused on their 
responsibilities rather than the overall completion and utilization of the 
project. This indicates a clear lack of decisive action or accountability and 
reflects a lack of urgency and proper oversight from the Ministry. 
Consequently, the Committee urges the Ministry to fix accountability on 
the involved officials and to review systemic errors in the procedures. 
  
  
  
Consultative mechanism to iron out land related issues 
  
Paragraph 3 of PAC Report No. 93 (17th Lok Sabha) 
  
10.   Noting from audit observation, the Committee find that due to non-commissioning 
of the ROBs and non-closure of Level Crossings Central Railways further incurred an 
avoidable expenditure of Rs. 1.04 crore towards pay and allowances of Gatemen 
manning the two LCs in addition to the expenditure on maintenance of these LCs for the 
period April 2017 to December 2021. Besides, Railway would continue to incur the 
expenditure on manning and maintenance of LCs until their closure. Though the State 
government also started the work in 2012 but work couldn't be completed as few issues 
in land acquisitions surfaced. From the submissions of the Ministry, the Committee note 
that there is no failure in following the system and following the procedure laid down. 
The Committee are of the view that the Ministry should have ensured the 
commensurate progress by the PWD before execution of work. The Committee are of 

7 
 
the view that most of the ROB infrastructure projects face challenges relating to land 
acquisition and right-of-way for construction. ROBs often require substantial land area 
and acquiring private properties and negotiating with landowners can be time 
consuming and complex. Legal and administrative procedures have to be followed to 
ensure fair compensation to the parties so as to minimize the possibility of disputes. For 
this, planning and coordination with local authorities as also shareholders is necessary 
with a view to effectively ironing out the difficulties. The Committee opine that MoR, 
while preparing the detailed project should invariably consult the local elected 
representatives and also consider appointment of consultants to oversee the planning 
and coordination with local authorities/landowners so that such projects do not suffer 
delays due to land acquisition/right of way related disputes. The Committee are also of 
the view that the Ministry of Railways need to henceforth explore the possibility of 
arriving at a cost sharing agreement with the concerned State Government and 
thereafter pay the full cost in the first instance and realize the State's share of the cost 
alongside the execution of work and deposit the amount so realized in a dedicated 
account for the project. This would not only ensure completion of work in time but would 
also rationalize cost sharing agreements between the Railway administration and the 
concerned State(s). The Committee desire to be apprised of the latest status in the 
matter.

cost sharing agreement has been minimized. The Committee, while appreciating 
the steps taken by the Ministry in this regard, desire that latest status of action 
taken in compliance with the recommendation be apprised to the Committee.

ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
The Committee note from audit observation that despite Ministry of Railways directives 
of May 2008, Central Railway Administration did not obtain the requisite Undertakings 
from the State Government in case of both the ROBs and executed the work of ROBs 
without ensuring the commensurate progress by the State PWD. As a result, the ROBs 
could not be commissioned even after a lapse of four years after completion of 
Railway's portion of the work of bridge proper and Capital expenditure of Rs 18.75 crore 
incurred by Railway Administration on the above two ROBs remain blocked due to non-
completion of approach portion of ROBs by PWD. Work of construction of the two ROBs 
was to be completed within a period of 18 months from the date of commencement of 
work. However, in both the cases, work could not be completed even after seven years 
after commencement and Level Crossings (LCs) could not be closed. From the 
submissions of the Ministry, the Committee note that Consent of cost sharing and 
closure of level crossing after construction of ROB had been taken from the state 
government and the Railway had started the portion of ROB within Railway boundary in 
2014 and would have possibly been completed by October, 2016. The Committee are of 
the view that the requisite undertaking for timely completion of work and encumbrance 
free land should have been taken from the State Government in case of both the ROBs. 
The Committee also desire that the Ministry need to find out the officers responsible for 
not undertaking the necessary consultation process before executing the project and 
apprise the Committee of the action taken, if any of the officials in this regard 
 
[Observations/Recommendation No. 2 of 93rd Report of the Public  
Accounts Committee (17thLokSabha)] 
 
 
Action taken 

10 
 
 “The Ministry of Railways directives were issued in May 2008 after sanction of 
Road Over Bridge in lieu of LC no. 99-A (Sanction year 1996). Consent of cost 
sharing and consent of level crossing gate closure was taken in the year 2011-12 
and 1996-97 respectively. Railway started the work of construction of ROBs after 
start of work in the approaches of both ROBs by State Govt. The start of the work 
in the approaches is sufficient to prove their priority for the work and commitment 
towards early land acquisition. Therefore, Railway took up the work for 
completion more of less simultaneously with the completion of the State Portion. 
Land acquisition is one of the major constraints in construction of the Road Over 
Bridge. The state government had been requested to expedite and complete the 
work in approaches as fast as possible but land acquisition is a time consuming 
and complex process, hence there is no specific undertaking of time period to 
complete the work of approaches. Due to delay in work of approaches in state 
portion, state government was chased regularly by Central Railway through 
letters as mentioned in table given below.”

many years due to a court case in land acquisition issue. The same has already

Observation/Recommendation 
Noting from audit observation, the Committee find that due to non-commissioning of the 
ROBs and non-closure of Level Crossings Central Railways further incurred an 
avoidable expenditure of Rs. 1.04 crore towards pay and allowances of Gatemen 
manning the two LCs in addition to the expenditure on maintenance of these LCs for the 
period April 2017 to December 2021. Besides, Railway would continue to incur the 
expenditure on manning and maintenance of LCs until their closure. Though the State 
government also started the work in 2012 but work couldn't be completed as few issues 
in land acquisitions surfaced. From the submissions of the Ministry, the Committee note 
that there is no failure in following the system and following the procedure laid down. 
The Committee are of the view that the Ministry should have ensured the 
commensurate progress by the PWD before execution of work. The Committee are of 
the view that most of the ROB infrastructure projects face challenges relating to land 
acquisition and right-of-way for construction. ROBs often require substantial land area 
and acquiring private properties and negotiating with landowners can be time 
consuming and complex. Legal and administrative procedures have to be followed to 
ensure fair compensation to the parties so as to minimize the possibility of disputes. For 
this, planning and coordination with local authorities as also shareholders is necessary 
with a view to effectively ironing out the difficulties. The Committee opine that MoR, 
while preparing the detailed project should invariably consult the local elected 
representatives and also consider appointment of consultants to oversee the planning 
and coordination with local authorities/landowners so that such projects do not suffer 
delays due to land acquisition/right of way related disputes. The Committee are also of 
the view that the Ministry of Railways need to henceforth explore the possibility of 
arriving at a cost sharing agreement with the concerned State Government and 
thereafter pay the full cost in the first instance and realize the State's share of the cost 
alongside the execution of work and deposit the amount so realized in a dedicated 
account for the project. This would not only ensure completion of work in time but would 
also rationalize cost sharing agreements between the Railway administration and the 
concerned State(s). The Committee desire to be apprised of the latest status in the 
matter. 
 
[Observations/Recommendation No. 3 of 93rd Report of the Public

acquisition. Therefore, Railway took up the work for completion more or less 
simultaneously with the completion of the State Portion. Legal and administrative 
procedures have also been followed in this case to ensure fair compensation to 
the parties. Similarly, planning and co-ordination of the Road crossing works is
